talks.title: 2026: Chris Bore - Colour Monsters, and Listening to Vicky
talks.teaser: A former manager reflects on missed warning signs and how preschool emotional-intelligence tools could strengthen workplace trust.
talks.summary:
Chris Bore opens with a story from 1984, when he was a general manager at a software publishing company and did not notice that his personal assistant was crying. He later came to see her as a weak point in the attack surface: someone who could have been befriended, or who could have become an insider threat. He argues that security programmes tend to treat people as assets to control or as risks to monitor.

He then draws on his work at a preschool, where the Colour Monsters emotional intelligence tool helps children name feelings and regulate them. Staff also use coloured armbands so that adults can signal they are struggling without having to explain why. He contrasts this with information security standards and workplace wellbeing standards, which he says focus on controlling people or reducing stress rather than on listening. He also describes monitoring ideas such as checking email start times or tone, and argues these intrude on privacy. A nursery abuse case, in which parents and staff raised concerns that went unactioned for about two years, shows that trained staff can still miss warning signs.

He concludes that the key is culture: an environment of trust where people can say they are not well without being judged, and where leaders check in with care. In the question round he suggested that manager training helps, but that caring and making room for others matters most. His takeaway is that colleagues need to feel safe enough to speak up.

talks.title: 2026: Ehren Osborne - Please, oh please, stick to the RFCs
talks.teaser: A penetration tester shows how ignoring HTTP and related RFCs creates parser gaps, host-header issues, and exploitable app behavior.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with everyday pentest frustrations: backends that return HTTP 200 for failed operations and front ends that obscure errors in JSON. That anecdote leads into what RFCs are and why HTTP 1.1 standards matter for consistent, testable behavior across proxies, CDNs, and application servers.

The core material walks through specification-backed attack surface. HTTP 1.1 rules on content length versus transfer encoding underpin request smuggling when implementations disagree. Host header requirements (missing, duplicate, or malformed values should yield 400) are often ignored, enabling discrepancies between reverse proxies and backends. A rapid-fire section covers phone number formats, email local-part case sensitivity, comments, and quoting—edge cases parsers mishandle, with a nod to email-splitting research.

War stories ground the advice: reflected arbitrary host values including script payloads on a legacy login page; a report download feature that accepted a crafted mime type parameter, enabling CRLF injection and response-splitting class risks, still pending vendor/CVE resolution after pushback. The closing plea is for developers and testers to read RFCs to reduce parser mismatches and discover legitimate-but-unusual inputs worth probing.

talks.title: 2026: Lauren Spokes - The Forensic War on Privacy Advances: Mobile Phones
talks.teaser: Explores how smartphone encryption, screen locks, and anti-theft features complicate law-enforcement digital forensics workflows.
talks.summary:
Every major smartphone privacy update shifts what investigators can recover from seized devices. The presentation opens by contrasting before-first-unlock and after-first-unlock states, where most user data stays encrypted until a PIN or biometric succeeds, and explains how full-disk encryption on older hardware differed from per-file keys on newer phones, including longer brute-force timelines and weaker recovery of deleted content.

On iOS, stolen device protection and hidden application folders tie sensitive changes to familiar locations, biometrics, and mandatory delays, which blocks many lab preparation steps when a handset has never been at the station. Android private space, strengthened anti-theft, upcoming on-device live threat detection, and mark-as-lost modes can interrupt client-based extractions, force biometric unlock, or cut networking when devices sit in backlog. Distress PINs, remote wipe, lockdown-style modes, and automatic reboots after 72 hours of inactivity add further pressure to isolate phones quickly and finish legal workflows in tight windows.

Practitioners should expect AFU devices to remain the primary target, plan for vendor-dependent workarounds as platforms evolve, and weigh manual device review or disclosed credentials against shrinking options when suspects withhold PINs on current-generation hardware.

talks.title: 2026: Ken Munro - Securing the connected skies...
talks.teaser: Explains why aircraft cannot be hacked from passenger seats and how avionics, flight bags and GPS have been tested.
talks.summary:
The talk reviews what has been learned about aircraft security over the past six or seven years. The speaker explains why attacking flight systems from a passenger seat is not realistic: the aircraft network is split into segregated domains, and the flight control domain is isolated, with only a one-way feed for the moving map. He also surveys the data buses in use, from ARINC 429 and the inductively coupled ARINC 629 to AFDX Ethernet on newer types.

The middle section walks through real cases. Researchers found that a Boeing electronic flight bag performance calculator lacked client-side validation, so runway length could be changed, and that a kiosk on a retrofitted 747 could be escaped to reach a default password. An Airbus-supplied app had disabled transport security, which allowed traffic to be intercepted. A recent paper showed that brief physical access to the avionics bay could inject flight plan and weight data. GPS spoofing was shown to corrupt other onboard systems, and a time jump forced reflashing of units that kept one aircraft out of service for nearly two weeks.

The closing section argues that mistakes in weight, runway and load data have caused real incidents, so software integrity matters for safety. The speaker says certified software makes disclosure slow, often a year or two, and advises researchers to coordinate with manufacturers and regulators. He points to the Defcon aerospace village as a place where this research is growing.

talks.title: 2026: Rand0h
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in 2026: Rand0h - It Takes A Hardware Village.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation delivered at a cybersecurity conference in Glasgow (Hack Glasgow), speaker Danny (known widely as "Rand0h") recounts his journey of designing and manufacturing his first custom hardware electronic conference badge. Built to celebrate the 10th anniversary of DEF CON's meme-driven contest "Whose Slide Is It Anyway?", the badge is modeled directly after the contest's iconic 4-foot etched symphonic gong. While walking through the technical hardware architecture, software development, and fabrication pitfalls, Rand0h emphasizes the human side of "Badge Life"—underscoring how community mentorship, peer support, and perseverance enabled a non-coder to bring an ambitious hardware concept from a napkin sketch to a 125-unit production run.

### Key Topics
- **Origins and Lore of "Whose Slide Is It Anyway?":** Originating as a variant of slideshow roulette where presenters speak to unseen meme-heavy slides, the contest evolved over a decade at DEF CON. The contest integrated a physical symphonic gong used by judges to disqualify participants, which directly inspired the badge's thematic design.
- **Learning Curve and Electronics Fundamentals:** Starting with minimal hardware experience, assembling LEGO lighting kits, and completing multiple Hacker Boxes (such as the 20-panel icosahedron "Tessellate"), Rand0h practiced surface-mount device (SMD) soldering and iterative breadboarding concepts via educational resources such as DigiKey and "30 Days Lost in Space."
- **AI-Assisted Engineering Workflow:** Relying on Claude (both claude.ai and Claude Code) to "vibe code" and bridge knowledge gaps in Python, C, and C++, the speaker developed 764 lines of code covering 44 functions. However, the talk highlights critical AI limitations, such as hallucinated PCB trace layouts, unworkable schematics, and incorrect pin assignments.
- **Manufacturing, Assembly, and Logistics:** Navigating PCB fabrication platforms (PCBWay, JLCPCB), ordering custom component reels, handling tariffs, and coordinating with an assembly line in Kansas City (Malmet) utilizing pick-and-place machines and automated solder paste printing.

### Technical Details
- **Microcontroller & Audio Architecture:** The badge runs on an ESP32-C3 microcontroller. Audio playback uses a W25 flash memory chip providing 8 MB of storage containing downsampled audio tracks. The ESP32 reads audio data and clocks it out to a MAX audio amplifier chip driving an onboard speaker.
- **Lighting and Interface:** The badge integrates 24 peripheral LEDs in a chained configuration along with 3 physical interactive buttons.
- **Interactive Features & Connectivity:** The device stores five base songs (with custom tracks programmed for early buyers), cycling audio snippets and memes. A specific audio sequence triggers an onboard Wi-Fi access point hosting a secret web server containing blogs, clues, and hidden challenges.
- **Failure Analysis & Design Flaws:** 
  - A footprint mismatch caused by an AI pinout hallucination on the MAX audio amplifier package bridged the 5V rail (powering LEDs and the amplifier) into the 3.3V rail (dedicated to ESP32 logic), causing voltage to creep upward and destroying downstream components.
  - The development required three major revision cycles, resolving severe battery drain through multiple firmware rewrites days before DEF CON.

### Takeaways
- **AI as a Tool, Not an Engineer:** Generative AI is a powerful assistant for rapid prototyping and firmware development, but builders must verify schematics, read manufacturer data sheets, and understand the core behavior of their designs.
- **Community and Collaboration:** Complex hardware projects require collective mentorship. Friends and experienced community members (such as Blinkster and one_dark_one) were indispensable in fixing schematics, routing traces, creating artwork, and performing quality assurance.
- **Resilience Against Scope Creep and Logistics:** First-time hardware designers should expect delays, avoid late scope additions (like physical vibration hit sensors), order surplus boards to account for component loss, and accept that real-world troubleshooting happens hands-on at the workbench.

talks.title: 2026: Gabrielle Hempel - Redlining the SOC: The Need for Speed in Cyber Defense
talks.teaser: Shows how SOC process delays, not tooling, let attackers move faster, and how to close those gaps.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a security operations center rarely fails because of a weak tool. Delays in triage, enrichment, approvals and handoffs give attackers time to move, and attack timelines are compressing. The speaker cites figures from the talk: an average e-crime breakout time of 29 minutes, a fastest observed breakout of 27 seconds, an 89% rise in AI-enabled adversary activity, and 82% of detections being malware-free. Planning should start from the assumption that attackers already have some access.

A ransomware case from a previous customer, a Fortune 500 company, anchors the talk. The EDR flagged suspicious PowerShell one minute after execution and the SIM received the alert immediately, but the alert sat in a triage queue for 23 minutes. It had no asset criticality, user context or threat scoring, so the analyst escalated slowly. By the time containment began, the attacker had moved laterally and started encrypting data, for a total dwell time of 41 minutes. The lesson was missing context and unclear ownership rather than ignored alerts.

The proposed fixes centre on detecting behaviour rather than relying only on indicators, and enriching alerts before triage so the analyst has context at the decision point. Automation should be driven by confidence rather than severity, with humans kept in the loop for critical assets and reversible actions built in as brakes. Identity, cloud and SaaS count as speed surfaces that need visibility. The talk closes by urging teams to feed every incident and analyst decision back into the next detection, enrichment step or playbook.
